extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IPR practitioners, parties in inter partes review (petitioners/respondents), and patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Evidentiary and legal standards used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board to evaluate obviousness, printed-publication/public accessibility, motivation to combine, expert testimony credibility, and related issues in an inter partes review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of the evidence standard for IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner has proved by a preponderance of the evidence that claim [X] would have been obvious over [references].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the governing evidentiary standard in the IPR for establishing obviousness and other asserted invalidity grounds; the Board repeatedly states outcomes as satisfied or not satisfied 'by a preponderance of the evidence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / public accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is publicly accessible if 'persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter or art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it.' (Acceleration Bay, LLC v. Activision Blizzard Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uploading a document to a website may be 'technically accessible' but not necessarily 'publicly accessible.' For a web-uploaded document, petitioner must present evidence that a POSITA could have reasonably found the website and then the document on that website using reasonable diligence. Indexing/cataloging is not required if the site's own search functions would have allowed a POSITA to find it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for printed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, 'the petitioner bears the burden of establishing by a preponderance of the evidence that a particular document is a printed publication.' (Nobel Biocare Servs. AG v. Instradent USA, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner must supply affirmative evidence showing public accessibility and cannot rely on absence of contrary proof from Patent Owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A motivation to combine 'can be found explicitly or implicitly in the prior art references themselves, in market forces, in design incentives, or in "any need or problem known in the field of endeavor at the time of invention and addressed by the patent."' (Forest Labs. quoting Arctic Cat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation need not be express; it can be implicit, based on market forces or known problems. The Board will consider the references and surrounding context; KSR applies: 'A person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires a reasonable expectation of success in combining references; mere possibility is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board considers predictability of the art and interchangeability of elements (e.g., in computer systems) as supporting a reasonable expectation. Petitioners need not show line-by-line code changes or bodily incorporation; general teachings that would enable a POSITA to implement the modification can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art disclosure that discourages the modification or combination at issue (i.e., 'teaches away') weighs against finding obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contentions that a reference 'teaches away' must be persuasive and supported by the prior art; generalized arguments about added complexity or space/processing costs are insufficient if the prior art already discloses related features or if the modification is consistent with the art's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term construction / breadth of claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are construed from the specification and context; e.g., 'The term "information processing apparatus" is broad and can be met by any number of information processing components.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claim-language can be met by multiple types of devices (personal computer, remote server, etc.); parties must explain why terms require narrower constructions, supported by specification or prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board adopts a concrete POSITA definition for analysis (here: one who would have had a bachelor’s degree in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Computer Engineering, or a related field, and two years of practical experience in digital data management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The POSITA definition is used to assess what references would have taught, what a skilled person would search for, and whether references were publicly accessible or readily usable; parties should propose and support a realistic POSITA level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must show why a POSITA would be interested in/seek the reference
rubrics_metrics.description: To argue that a web document would have been located by a POSITA, petitioner must explain why such a person would have been interested in the product or information (i.e., why they would look on that website).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General assertions that products were 'well known' are insufficient; show nexus (e.g., citations in contemporaneous patents, market prominence, or other evidence) that would have driven a POSITA to the site or document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must show how a POSITA would locate the document on the website with reasonable diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must present evidence that a skilled person could reasonably find the website and then the document thereon using ordinary diligence (Samsung Elecs. Co. v. Infobridge Pte. Ltd.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations or testimony identifying the navigation path, site search functionality, or contemporaneous indexing help; claiming 'found in three clicks' requires showing those clicks reflect natural POSITA behavior and reasonable diligence rather than guided or artificial navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of arguments (no new theories in reply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments or theories first presented in a Reply (e.g., a new theory of publication by distribution with product sales) may be untimely and declined by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should present their full theory and supporting evidence in the Petition or Response; belated theories raised only in reply risk being disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and sufficiency of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony must be supported by the cited portions of the prior art and consistent with the record; conclusory or unsupported expert assertions may be discredited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will compare expert testimony against the intrinsic and extrinsic evidence (e.g., cited patent passages, exhibits). Inconsistencies or failure to explain why citations support the expert's conclusions reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unworkability / suitability is more than superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing that an alternative is 'better' (e.g., wired has superior speed/security) is not sufficient to prove that the alternative renders the claimed approach unworkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To defeat obviousness on grounds of unworkability, Patent Owner must show the alternative would be truly unworkable in the claimed context; mere vulnerabilities or performance disadvantages do not establish unworkability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of distribution or sales to show publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If asserting that a manual or document was published via distribution with product sales, petitioner must present evidence of actual distribution/sales and that the document accompanied those sales before the critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An untimely or unsupported claim of distribution (e.g., first presented in reply without sales figures or contemporaneous records) will not satisfy the printed-publication burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability/interchangeability in the art supports combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictability of the technological field and known interchangeability of system elements support a finding that combining teachings of references would have been predictable and successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the art (e.g., computer systems, GUIs) is predictable and elements are commonly interchanged, the Board may find a reasonable expectation of success and obviousness even without a specific implementation path provided in the references.
